Don't Ask, Do Tell! An Oral History of the Clinton Congress

Michael Davis

Michael Davis

Michael Davis   Assistant Professor of English at Le Moyne college in Syracuse, New York. He completed his dissertation, “Mona Lisa's Modernity: Queer Theories through Pater and Freud,” at the University of Virginia in 1997 and is currently completing a book on Virginia Woolf entitled Dating Mrs. Dalloway: Self-Reflexion, Suicide, and the Ends of Fiction.

In this essay I attempt to trace a particular sequence of sexual-cultural-political events over the course of about a decade from 1989 to 1999, the period roughly corresponding to the rise and rule of the Clinton presidency, and to thereby demonstrate the playing out of a particular plot of desire, and to offer up a particular narrative that I hope might have some explanatory power, the power to explain how and why certain events acquired the significance that they did, what pressing cultural function such events served, and how we might connect one event to another in meaningful terms. Although it may already be obvious from my use of this opening trope, I should say here at the outset that I am by training a scholar of literature and specifically of narrative theory and of the relationship between narrative and sexuality, not only of how narrative, both fictional and historical, can be a function of sexuality, but also of how sexuality can be a function of narrative. In the pages that follow I draw broadly on a wide range of plots and narrative structures in my readings of cultural events and the relationships among them, and similarly and simultaneously, on a wide range of theories of sexuality in those readings. But I draw most significantly on the theories of Freud and Foucault, arguably the two major theorists of sexuality of the twentieth century, and take up what might seem an implausible theoretical position halfway between them. From Freud's Interpretation of Dreams I take not only an understanding of the way in which the conscious creates, through a process of repression, an unconscious, but also what remains to me a legitimate hermeneutic method, a set of reading practices, through which to understand the workings of the unconscious and at least the dynamics of repressed desire. It will be apparent, then, that I do not wholly embrace Foucault's polemical critique, in The History of Sexuality: An Introduction, of what he calls Freud's “repressive hypothesis” (10). Rather, I would suggest that that reactionary critique is largely Foucault's way of differentiating himself from Freud and of individuating as a powerful theorist in his own right. Indeed, there are several points in The History of Sexuality: An Introduction where Foucault backs off a bit from his strong claim that repression does not exist, at one point disclaiming, “I do not maintain that the prohibition of sex is a ruse,” suggesting more mildly that we should, rather, shift our analysis from the prohibition of sex to what he sees as the many discourses of sexuality that our culture has, perhaps paradoxically, simultaneously produced: to shift our field of inquiry from the mechanisms of repression and from the realm of the repressed to those more apparent and more accessible speech acts concerning sexuality, for which Foucault provides, if only by way of example, a complementary reading practice.

Socialism: Utopian and Melancholic?

Colin Campbell

Colin Campbell

Colin Campbell   Currently pursuing a Ph. D. in the Graduate Programme in Social and Political Thought, York University, Toronto. This paper is a re-visitation of his M.A. Thesis, “Imagining the Possible: The Critical Theory of Herbert Marcuse,” completed under the auspices of the programme in Contemporary Social and Political Thought at the University of Victoria.

Melancholy Democracy

According to Freud, melancholia is a process by which love for an object is denied or foreclosed, where that denial and foreclosure persist internally, in the subject of that denial. A loved object whose existence is disavowed becomes, in effect, a part of the subject. The process is distinguished from mourning precisely in the fact that its object is nowhere to be found; instead of grief for the person lost, there is an almost ritualized self-abasement, guilt without shame. According to Freud, what begins as “a mental constellation of revolt … has then by a certain process, passed over into the crushed state of melancholia” (Freud 586).

Judith Butler argues that the elementary function of melancholia in subject-formation has determinate consequences at every level of the socio-linguistic, and therefore political, field. The performativity of discourse, as it appears in Bodies That Matter, sets a real limit on the political agency of the subject in relation to social power. While it has been misread in criticisms of Gender Trouble as a capacity of the gendered subject to choose his/her gender like a garment (Bodies x), performativity is not the expression of a human will in language. Discursive effects are not objects fixed by subjects, but vectors of social power, phenomena which confound conventional cause-effect thinking. Bodies are materialized along these vectors, as the sediment of the historicity of norms, but bodies are far from being stable objects. Their form of materiality is never complete, is always grounded in a partial disavowal of the body's materializable desires.

The vicissitudes of materiality play out in the wider social and political field. Any political identity-claim is produced by the foreclosure of another bodily materiality that would threaten it; an alien, immaterial materiality, its shadow. But this threat to identity is not only a “something” that is external to it, but is also precisely the impossibility of the attempt to expel that which will always be inherent to it. It is in fact the case, then, that “discourse fails to totalize the social field” (Bodies 192). Any attempt to secure the social field through a totalizing reading is nevertheless inherently traumatic.

On Reading Freud with My 14-Year-Old Son

Harvey Lieberman

Harvey Lieberman

Harvey Lieberman   Clinical psychologist, is executive vice president of the Institute for Community Living in New York City.

It is past 9 p. m. on a Sunday evening, and my 14-year-old son prances into the kitchen where my wife and I are lingering over dessert. He is dressed in accordance with his notions of style—backward pointing baseball cap with loose pants. He's been home only 15 minutes after having spent the day at a friend's house. His visit with us coincides with a TV commercial break.

“Dad, do we have a biography around the house I can use for school?” He briskly asks.

“What's your assignment?” I answer. My voice is tinged with more than a little suspicion because my eighth grader generally doesn't want me to butt into his academic business unless he is in trouble.

“We have to read a biography—it can be about anybody—and do a report on it.”

“Your mother or I will be glad to take you to the library tomorrow. I don't think we have anything much around.”

“No! My teacher wants us to bring a book in tomorrow. I know we have a book I can use.”

“Okay, okay, I'll look. This could be a problem for you to work out with your teacher. I'm sure there is nothing here suitable for your reading level.”

I search through our bookshelves overflowing with volumes purchased before my wife and I decided that we must be more selective in how we use our limited space. I return to my son's side with two books. I extend forth my hand to show him one book and proceed to describe it.

“This one, Young Man Luther, is by Erik Erikson. He was one of Freud's great followers. He writes about Martin Luther. Luther was a real rebel, the first Protestant. He went up against the abuses of the Catholic Church at a time when it took tremendous courage to do that. It's a big book and although easier than this other one, we will need to read it together for you to understand it. I don't think you can finish within the time you have.”

“What's the other book?” he asks.

“It's Freud's study of Leonardo da Vinci. It's only 100 pages and very hard. You'll need my help with this one too. Your teacher may not accept it; it is not a detailed biography. At times, you've asked me about Freud's theories. Here they are in original form.

A Lacanian Approach to Ethno-National Conflict: The Case of Northern Ireland

Adrian Millar

Adrian Millar

Adrian Millar   Assistant lecturer at the Department of Sociology, National University of Ireland, Dublin (University College Dublin). He completed a doctorate in Japanese at the Centre for East Asian Studies at the University of Sheffield (1988) and a doctorate in the Department of Politics at University College Dublin (1999). He also held a Government of Ireland postdoctoral fellowship at the Department of Politics, UCD, and was an honorary research fellow in the Institute for British-Irish Studies at the University.

Introduction

At its core, the conflict in Northern Ireland is not about religion or political insecurity over sovereignty or boundaries per se. Instead it is about two communities trying to expand their economic, political, cultural, and religious sense of self. Thus, the conflict is best understood as resulting from the interplay of the imaginary, symbolic, and real at the heart of subjectivity. How people construct their communal identity or interpret themselves is mainly unconscious, and the rationalizations this involves are the key to analysis of the conflict. The institutionalization of rationalizations involved in the interplay of these three orders reinforces communal division and prolongs antagonism. Interests become a focus of violent conflict when one's own aggression is rationalized as attack by the other and neuroses are badly handled.

Outline

I begin by presenting a brief examination of the literature on the republican and loyalist communities in Northern Ireland. This literature review suggests that there is a need to go beyond an examination simply of how people positively interpret themselves to a more critical and searching examination of the unconscious dynamics in the constitution of political identities. I then present an outline of Lacanian key to analysis of the conflict. The institutionalisation of rationalisations involved in the interplay of these three orders reinforces communal division and prolongs antagonism. Interests become a focus of violent conflict when one's own aggression is rationalised as attack by the other and neuroses are poorly handled.

Psychoanalysis and My Research Methodology

In my section on findings, I attempt to identify some typical republican and loyalist communal meanings and their rationalisations that contribute to the reproduction of relations of domination. In my conclusion I point out the relevance of Lacanian analysis to the management of ethno-national conflicts. I end with a series of recommendations.

The Literature

My reading of the general literature on Northern Ireland makes it clear that there is a gap regarding a serious exploration of the self-interpretation of republicans, and to a lesser degree, of loyalists. Those materials that have the most relevance for the present research are works that highlight in some way the community dimension of the conflict and the role of the Republican and Loyalist communities in particular. Among these are McGarry and O'Leary Explaining Northern Ireland (1995), Ruane and Todd The Dynamics of Conflict in Northern Ireland (1996), O'Connor's In Search of a State: Catholics in Northern Ireland (1993) and Northern Protestants: an Unsettled People by Susan McKay (2000). These works are more thorough in this regard than anything previously published on the Catholic or Protestant communities. McGarry and O'Leary's work has the added value of showing us the shortcomings of the narrower political science approach, which fails to account for the deeper meanings of political identity. Particular conceptual categories which Ruane and Todd use, such as oppositional differences, the cultural, religious, and political treatment of the conflict, and the redemptive resolution of the conflict, make them highly relevant. O'Connor's work is relevant on the grounds that while it deals exclusively and highly effectively with the Catholic community, its journalistic approach also enables us to identify the need for a strong methodology in an examination of political identity. The same can be said of McKay in relation to the Protestant community.

The Phantasy of Being Cured: Thoughts on Psychoanalysis and Historical Interpretation

James Glass

James Glass

James Glass   Professor of Government and Politics at the University of Maryland, College Park. His most recent book, “Life Unworthy of Life”: Mass Murder in Hitler's Germany, looks at the power of medical imagery and science in motivating genocide. He is currently working on a project examining the role of civil society in encouraging mass murder in Nazi Germany, and what group psychoanalytic theory offers in the way of understanding transgressive and psychotic violence.

Introduction: Culture and Belief

The ability of cultures to wage mass murder depends on two fundamental factors: (1) a willingness of the population to accept such behavior as legitimate and (2) the normalizing of mass murder as essential national policy. Each of these factors in turn depends on the capacity of groups to internalize the belief structure necessary for action and to reach consensus on the methods necessary to implement beliefs. Psychoanalytic group theory brings us at least a step closer to understanding how this process works; it is simply not enough to argue that, in the case of Nazi Germany it was Hitler's decision or the party's “madness,” or, with September 11th, that it was bin Laden's charisma alone. Each instance of mass murder—the murder of European Jews, the deaths of thousands of innocents in the World Trade Center and the Pentagon—a group-willed set of beliefs was essential for carrying out these policies. Masses of individuals, organized into collectives or groups, needed to hold these ends not as just rational calculation but as willed belief. Group phantasy articulates the perception; the very existence of individuals, their bodies, demands annihilation, extermination, purification. In Germany, Jews and gypsies constitute this hated, impure Other; for the al Qaeda network, despised otherness appears as the Americans, Western values, the pleasures of the body. Where can we turn in group psychology theory for light that illuminates the causality behind these actions?

Claudio Neri, an Italian psychoanalyst and a professor of Group Psychology at the University of Rome, offers provocative insights. Neri draws inspiration from Didier Anzieu, a French psychoanalyst and theorist of group behavior. Anzieu uses concepts like group illusion and the group as a container; he introduces the concept of the Skin Ego, which I will return to in a moment. Neri elaborates the idea that illusions tie groups together. And the group itself acts as a container for powerful, explosive feelings and channels those feelings into action. Neri's own conclusions are derived from watching small groups in action, but I believe we can use his theory to make certain generalizations about large-group behavior, or the behavior of what I call “culture-groups”—loose associations of various groups within a given cultural field, united by an overriding ideological commitment. Neri's small-group psychology offers a beginning point from which to explain action and behavior on a larger scale. I should also add that Neri draws from Wilfred Bion; but for my purposes, his theoretical elaborations of Anzieu are more relevant to the kinds of political groups engaged in ongoing activities of mass murder.

State Terrorism and Psychic Trauma in Latin America

Nancy Hollander PHD

Nancy Hollander

Nancy Hollander   Member and on the faculty of the Psychoanalytic Center of California in Los Angeles and Professor of Latin American and Women's History at California State University, Dominguez Hills. She is author of Love in a Time of Hate: Liberation Psychology in Latin America (Rutgers University Press, 1997) and numerous articles on the psychological effects of political repression. She is in private practice in Los Angeles, CA

Almost three decades ago, on September 11, 1973, Chilean democracy was overthrown by a ruthless military coup. Since then, September 11 has been etched in the psyches of people throughout Latin America, a vivid symbol of suffering, pain, and loss (political repression). The coup launched a military dictatorship whose policies embodied what has come to be commonly accepted as the definition of terrorism, namely, “the use of force or the threat of force against civilian populations to achieve political objectives.” The Chilean military were not alone in this endeavor. From the 1960s through the 1980s, from Guatemala to Argentina, Latin America fell under the cruel domination of terrorist states that disappeared, tortured, and murdered hundreds of thousands of men, women, and children. Massive psychic trauma was suffered by citizens who lived in this persecutory environment, and it was exacerbated when the democratic governments that replaced military rule pardoned the former perpetrators for their extreme human rights abuses. Never having acknowledged their wrongdoing, the torturers walk freely among their victims/survivors in the cultures of impunity that characterize contemporary Latin American.

Today, the themes of impunity and psychic trauma associated with September 11 in Latin America resonate with another September 11. Suddenly in this country we are no longer immune from the fears and anxieties Latin Americans have lived with in an ongoing way as a result of terrorism in their countries. Their experience may by illuminating to us as we now struggle on a daily basis—with the end of life as we knew it, the loss of loved ones, the persecutory anxiety inherent in not knowing the nature of the next threat, the fears generated by living with unpredictability, the oscillation between hypervigilance and psychic numbing.

What was the nature of the experience under state terror and its insidious and ongoing traumatic impact? The global and cumulative nature of the collective trauma was due to the fact that it was organized by the state, whose entire apparatus of military, legal, educational, medical, mass media, and religious institutions cooperated in imposing an insidious culture of fear. The state's efforts were shored up by ideological and material support from the U. S. government and multinational corporations whose interests paralleled those of the military and elite classes. Under state terror, societies were divided into perpetrators, victims, and bystanders. Not only the men, women, and children whose raped, tortured, and massacred bodies were the victims of human rights abuses, but the entire society was the target of state terror. One of the Argentine Generals who carried out that country's “dirty war” put it this way: “First,” he warned ominously, “we are going to kill all of the subversives; then their collaborators; then their sympathizers; then the indifferent; and finally, the timid.

An Object Relations Theory of Prejudice

Lynne Layton

Lynne Layton

Lynne Layton   Assistant. Clinical Professor of Psychology at Harvard Medical School and teaches popular culture at Harvard University. She is co-editor of JPCS, a candidate at the Massachusetts Institute for Psychoanalysis, author of Who's That Girl? Who's That Boy? Clinical Practice Meets Postmodern Gender Theory, and co-editor, with Susan Fairfield and Carolyn Stack, of Bringing the Plague: Toward a Postmodern Psychoanalysis.

The following two papers, by Thomas Oberlechner and Ron Aviram respectively, introduce the ideas of Ronald Fairbairn. Aviram applies certain of Fairbairn's ideas to a study of prejudice, arguing that prejudice in some cases might be better explained by looking at character pathology rooted in developmental failures than by looking at social conditions. He draws interesting parallels between Fairbairn's work and empirical work on prejudice from social psychology. We are publishing Oberlechner's paper to give an audience unfamiliar with Fairbairn a more detailed introduction to his views on development, on a human nature motivated not by pleasure-seeking but by object seeking, on an unconscious that arises from relational failures, and on the nature of an ego multiply split in relation to its objects. As Oberlechner writes, paranoia, hysteria, obsessive compulsion, considered to be character types in classical theories, are for Fairbairn all defenses against a more basic schizoid condition. While Oberlechner's paper does not itself suggest how one might draw on Fairbairn's theory to address social issues, his introduction raises a possible challenge to Aviram's assumption that a Fairbairnian view of prejudice roots prejudice in individual rather than social pathology. As Oberlechner suggests at the end of his paper, where he considers the clinical implications of Fairbairn's theory, Fairbairn's “understanding of schizoid splitting and withdrawal mechanisms has helped define the narcissistic and borderline personality disorder.” Many psychoanalytic social critics have examined the connections between the demands of contemporary capitalism and the production and prevalence of narcissistic personality disorder (Lasch, Kovel, Livesay, Sloan, to name a few). Fairbairn's analysis of schizoid phenomena captures a complexity of narcissistic disorders that Kohut's work does not. Further, and with regard specifically to the understanding of prejudice, what Fairbairn describes clearly resonates with what Adorno and his coinvestigators contemporaneously identified as the authoritarian personality (which, in my view, has many as yet to be examined parallels with narcissistic personality disorder). With this in mind, one might draw on Fairbairn not only to understand individual developmental failures but also to investigate what kind of social structure is conducive to producing schizoid phenomena, including pathological prejudice.

In this short paper I want to try to conceptualize how the field of psychoanalysis, both as an intellectual, scholarly practice and as a clinical procedure, could be most effectively incorporated into a contemporary research university. This will necessarily entail discussing some of the reasons why such a move is necessary or at least worth thinking about; addressing some of the problems and obstacles that stand in the way of a smooth integration of psychoanalysis into the university setting; and finally picturing a new sort of relationship between psychoanalysis and the university that might lead to a renascence of our field with something like the excitement, fascination, explanatory power, and sheer pleasure that seem to us, perhaps nostalgically, to have characterized its early days, and perhaps also that accounted for our own initial attraction to it in the first place.

As for the reasons why this project calls to us, I can be brief. Organized psychoanalysis is in a crisis of confidence, in itself and in its relation to the public it serves. It is no longer able to look to the medical profession and to the medical schools to serve as its professional and institutional home and protector, nor does it enjoy the widespread faith in its legitimacy as an explanatory system or its efficacy as a therapy that it once did. The response of organized psychoanalysis in this country, as represented by the American Psychoanalytic Association (APsaA), has been to very rapidly repeal the requirement that candidates for psychoanalytic training must, with a few rare exceptions, be MD physicians with a residency in psychiatry, and to open access to training not only to PhD's in Clinical Psychology, but also to a variety of non-MD mental health professionals and practitioners, such as nurses, social workers, family counselors, and so on.

While this represents a liberalization of psychoanalysis and an expansion of its scope in a clinical direction, it does nothing in particular to address the intellectual project of psychoanalysis as one of the great scholarly discourses of the modern world. The APsaA has evolved into an organization bifurcated into a professional organization concerned with guild issues, and an educational institution setting and overseeing standards for training—essentially a vocational issue. It has no real institutional energy or structure devoted primarily to promoting psychoanalysis as a scholarly enterprise engaged in original thought and research, in conversation with other fields and disciplines whether among the sciences or the more humanistic areas of inquiry.

Freud and earlier generations of analysts were skeptical about teaching psychoanalysis in the university. They didn't view the university as an institution which embodied the values of objectivity and open inquiry, but saw it as a source of possible distortion and resistance to the findings of their controversial and fledgling discipline. While this sort of defensiveness may have made sense at one time, it also helped create the hermetic and dogmatic culture that has characterized many psychoanalytic institutes. And its continuation only serves to prolong the current crisis of professional psychoanalysis. For its own rejuvenation, our discipline must open itself to a broad interchange with the larger intellectual and scientific community.

At the same time as the profession of psychoanalysis has been experiencing a profound crisis, analysis as a non-clinical, academic subject has been growing in the university—flourishing in the newer cross-disciplinary fields such as Cultural Studies, Women's' Studies, Gender Studies, and Literary Theory. And here and there, it is even making its way into philosophy departments. Indeed, a new field of psychoanalytic studies—in which the members of this panel are involved—has even emerged over the last decade.

All of these developments are to be applauded. They can only help to move psychoanalysis away from the narrow pragmatic orientation of a professional guild, which characterized it for many years, back toward its original calling as a broadly based cultural movement. Nevertheless, there are still many vexing questions about the role of psychoanalysis in the university, and I would like to address two of them today. The first concerns the problem of transference, and the second, the problem of professional cultures.

(1) If we take education in its broadest sense—as character formation—then University learning and clinical psychoanalysis are both educational enterprises. Yet, they each seek to accomplish their educational goals in a very different way. As I will argue, the difference between them centers on the function of the transference. Psychoanalysis represents an institutionalized tradition that is more than a century old. The tradition comprises many vivid personalities, canonical texts, classical controversies, and juicy scandals. Its history—in which the personal and theoretical are thoroughly intertwined—presents such an engrossing story that students, particularly undergraduates, often find it fascinating. Indeed, this is one of the arguments its academic opponents often use against the teaching of psychoanalysis in the university. They claim it's too seductive and leads students away from the more arid domain of valid science.

At the “Psychoanalysis across the Disciplines” Conference in November 2001, several academics and psychoanalytic practitioners from the United Kingdom and from across the United States spoke at the plenary sessions about teaching psychoanalysis in their institutions. This short paper about teaching psychoanalysis in Higher Education is based on my contribution in one of the sessions, and reflects my own experiences of teaching in two very different settings in the UK. I teach on an MA in Psychoanalytic Studies at the Tavistock Clinic, and on the Psychosocial Studies undergraduate degree program at the University of East London, which contains a great deal of psychoanalysis. In what follows, I describe the two programs and look at how each involves consideration of some key questions concerning the teaching of psychoanalysis: what kind of a body of knowledge is psychoanalysis? The MA in Psychoanalytic Studies, housed in the Tavistock Clinic in Hampstead, is a stone's throw from Freud's English home in Maresfield Gardens. It is an affluent, literary, liberal neighborhood full of well-preserved Georgian and Edwardian houses. Something of this sense of privilege and of a secure heritage finds its way into the Tavistock Clinic itself, with photographs in the main corridors of British psychoanalytic luminaries involved with the Clinic, including Wilfred Bion, John Bowlby, and Enid Balint. The Clinic itself, though, is a National Health Service Trust, and is located in a nondescript 1950s utilitarian building that is unusually well-cared for, but smells and feels like a hospital. People coming and going through the doors are a mix of doctors, patients (who might be children, families, adolescents or adults), psychotherapists, and students (the categories are not mutually exclusive). The Trust is the leading public sector mental health training institution in the country and is trying to uphold its distinctively Kleinian and Object Relational psychoanalytic approach to the treatment of mental illness, in a political climate at best oblivious to its aims. The Clinic's informal motto is “no clinical services without training; no training without research; no research without clinical services,” which says something about the starting point in relation to psychoanalysis—that is, to start with psychoanalytic practice.

“Returning from the Future, to Read the Past, in Order to Understand the Present”

This volume of essays serves a three-fold purpose. First, it is an announcement of the Amsterdam School for Cultural Analysis (ASCA) as a new institutional player in the ever-expanding field of cultural studies. Second, it provides examples of the institute's theoretical positioning as the majority of the essays are based upon papers originally presented at the 1995 ASCA conference “A Practice of Cultural Analysis: A Workshop on Interdisciplinarity.” Third, and much more confusingly, it at times appears to be a call for “cultural analysis” as a corrective or alternative to the field of cultural studies. In the review that follows I will present the multiple issues exposed in this important collection and then address what I see as some of the problems in its understanding of cultural analysis.

The Practice of Cultural Analysis: Exposing Interdisciplinary Interpretation is edited and introduced by the esteemed cultural critic and founding director of the ASCA, Mieke Bal.1 Bal sets the ball rolling with an informative and exhilarating positioning of cultural analysis' role as “an interdisciplinary practice” that “seeks to understand the past as part of the present, as what we have around us, and without which no culture would be able to exist” (1). The challenge, according to Bal, is for this collection of essays to refute the view that “interdisciplinarity makes the object of inquiry vague and the methodology muddled” (2). As an initial attempt to explain these vague assertions, she turns to a Dutch graffito painted on a highway underpass during the 1980s. As a writer of art histories, Bal skillfully exposes the possible meanings of the public address to passing motorists (as well as for the artist and other authorities). The ambiguous message of the graffito, like many cultural artifacts, presents a problem to the reader in that we can never be sure exactly what was the author's intent/message. This graffito then serves as an example for practitioners of cultural analysis to remember that when we seek “to expose” meanings through our “close readings” or “public presentations,” perhaps the best method is to ask questions that seek to open up new readings instead of to close down the dialogue by constructing a final interpretation (4-5).

In her recent study on racial melancholia Anne Anlin Cheng asks, “How does an individual go from being a subject of grief to being a subject of grievance?” (3). In other words, how does one move “from suffering injury to speaking out against that injury”? (Cheng 3). This question is similarly at the heart of Frances L. Restuccia's Melancholics In Love: Representing Women's Depression and Domestic Abuse. Restuccia argues that melancholic and battered women have found ways out of suffering toward the healing process of grievance (also known as mourning) by engaging with artistic representations of depression and domestic abuse. The premise of Melancholies in Love is that for sufferers of depression and abuse, representation affords a kind of mourning by articulating previously unthinkable and unarticulated grief.

Restuccia's book, including two chapters never before published, traverses a range of female “melancholies in love” from classical novels (Austen's Emma and Persuasion), contemporary women's fiction (Anita Brookner's Look at Me, Margaret Atwood's Lady Oracle, Margaret Drabble's Jerusalem the Golden), mystical pornography (Pauline Réage's Story of O and Return to the Château), documentary film and photography (Defending Our Lives and Donna Ferrato's Living with the Enemy), and rock-star autobiography (Turner's I, Tina). These melancholic texts, Restuccia suggests, are nonetheless therapeutic for their subjects, readers, and authors. For by transferring “empirical violence” into discourse, artistic representation allows opportunities for non-violent engagement with the traumas of depression and domestic abuse. This engagement is crucial for the recovery of the melancholic or battered subject whose injury is “experienced as a breakdown in signification,” where she or he “loses a sense of the power of the signifier, having difficulties with thinking and speaking, ‘concatenating’ signs” (Clark 191-192). In Julia Kristeva's terms, this breakdown constitutes a loss of access to the symbolic (“asymbolia”). Representation, however, restores the subject to symbolization, the process of making meaning out of signs.

While psychoanalysis has been utilized as an effective means for critiquing the cultural strictures and regimes that attempt to normalize sexuality, in the epic theater of contemporary theory, Lacanian psychoanalysis has appeared most often in two reductive and mutually reinforcing roles. One is the universalizing and ahistorical psychoanalysis, a confusing and elusive but ultimately patriarchal and heteronormative law. The other is what Joan Copjec describes in her book Read My Desire: Lacan Against the Historicists as a “‘Foucauldization’ of Lacanian theory”: a Foucault-heavy synthesis of Michel Foucault's and Jacques Lacan's theorizations of sexuality (19). In both appearances, the radical potential of psychoanalysis' formulation of the unconscious and desire is occluded, repressed, or simply invisible. Tim Dean's ground-breaking study, Beyond Sexuality pulls the curtain down on these well-known performances and brings the act of actually reading Lacanian psychoanalysis psychoanalytically to center stage. In doing so, Dean reveals how a psychoanalytic understanding of Lacan's work can help transform and radicalize contemporary theorizations of sexual desires, practices, and identities, and then put those theorizations to politically progressive use.

Unlike many studies of psychoanalysis that too quickly fold back on their own discourses even as they theorize the relation between psychoanalysis and the social, Dean takes the reader through the necessary steps to show how a psychoanalytic understanding of the unconscious, which is thoroughly sexual, can positively effect the social dimensions of sexuality for the better. First, Dean articulates how immanent history and the social are to the psychoanalytic symbolic. And perhaps more importantly, he reminds us that Lacan's formulation of desire constitutes a conceptual outside that resists the reduction of history and the social to the images through which they appear. He then maps out specific and foreseeable ways that an understanding of psychoanalysis' necessarily difficult and counterintuitive theorizations of desire can help us ethically confront the most pressing contemporary social and sexual crisis, AIDS.

Incision as the Bar of Significations Incisions

An incision is a cut made by an instrument that marks the skin, opening up the body's inside from its outside, drawing blood as the skin's surface swells and becomes raw. Such a scoring by a knife or a stylus exposes us to the sight/site/cite1 of the Real, the psychic realm of the unconscious which Lacan claimed to be beyond language yet intimately dwelling within it. The Real is precisely where the signifier fails; where the Symbolic Order of language no longer holds. The Lacanian Real is “that before which the imaginary faltered, that over which the symbolic stumbles, that which is refractory, resistant” (Sheridan x). The incision produces a momentary trauma, a bodily memory which forces a slippage of signs that begins to change and modify the body's image.

Lacan inverted Saussure's algorithm for the linguistic sign with:

s signified

to show the primacy of the signifier over the signified. Here the bar, as the line that separates the word from its imaged-meaning, designates the impossibility of the signifier ever guaranteeing a correspondent or non-ambiguous meaning. Metaphorically this barred line is like an incision. The cosmetic surgeon's scalpel, or the piercer's needle forces the body's established image to unravel and come apart. The body's image begins to “slip.” In this sense acupuncture is a mild form of piercing where the body's nerve routes and electrical flows are redistributed to relieve pain as the morphogenic image of the body's memory is re-mapped.2

By using the flesh as a medium the Lacanian Real becomes inscribed in these piercings and cosmetic surgical operations whose effects are to psychically re-map and re-member the body differently, with sexually different bodies requiring different inscriptive tools to etch their different surfaces. Hence such extreme skin games are an attempt to challenge The Symbolic Order as it is currently defined by patriarchal and heterosexual dominance by an increasingly diverse range of middle-class enthusiasts.3 In each different case, however, the isomorphism of the inside and the outside of the body image—cathected with libidinal intensity so as to hold the body's Imaginary and Symbolic psychic registers together—are opened up, torn asunder, and anamorphically skewed to form another screen-image (see Adams). Pain awaits in the crevice that marks the inside from the outside, waiting to be opened up to leave a Real scar. The body begins its semiological slide into another imaginary when the “bar” of signification which holds the signifier to the signified begins to be incised by the etching tools like the surgical scalpel, the tattoo stylus, the hook, and the spike.

This essay considers the psychological appeal of the CBS reality show Survivor. The original draft of the essay was written before September 11. Several of my initial speculations about the show's appeal were thus based on social conditions that have now radically altered. The reality that gave rise to reality shows, in other words, is no longer the same. This fact does not affect my argument about the show's past appeal, but it does make me wonder about the public's continuing response to Survivor and its prospects for the future. There was definitely an element of weirdness when Survivor 3 debuted immediately following President Bush's press conference on our latest sallies into Afghanistan and reports of more terrorist threats at home. The juxtaposition only highlighted the fabricated, frivolous nature of Survivor's so-called “reality.” Yet the appeal of the show, I believe, lies less in its “reality” than in the underlying fantasies and conflicts it enacts and allows viewers to experience vicariously. The question in my mind now is whether the fantasies and relational conflicts Survivor exposes can be tolerated in the present atmosphere.

For those unfamiliar with Survivor, the basic scenario is this. Sixteen contestants (“castaways,” as they are called) are dropped off in an isolated environment (an island off the coast of Borneo in the first series, the Australian outback in the second, Africa in the third). They are divided into two teams, or “tribes.” Besides battling the elements and working to provide themselves with shelter and food, the tribes compete every few days in elaborately designed physical, and sometimes mental, challenges. One challenge rewards the victors with creature comforts or morale boosters, while the second and most important challenge excuses the winning tribe from having to attend a Tribal Council in which they must vote off one of their team members. The tribes eventually merge—former enemies now become teammates who are nevertheless competing against one another. When it comes down to the final two, contestants who were voted off after the merge return to form the Tribal Council jury, and the jury votes for the ultimate winner and recipient of the million-dollar prize.

The fact that homicides have thus far been conceptualized as an “event” indicates the existence of variables both intrinsic (motive) and extrinsic (luck/chance) to the chain of incidents leading to its “culmination.” Consequently, when both variables interact, the identities of the participants become unclear, since homicide may be an accidental effect of “sibling offense” rather than the fruition of substantial homicidal intention. To illustrate the nebulousness of categorical identities in homicide contexts, I used parricide as an example of homicide that subverts the meaning of signifiers such as “victim,” “hero,” and “father” (see Shon, “Desire”).

But there is another simple reason, in addition to making classificatory distinctions using psychoanalytic concepts, why parricide cases do not pose a problem for homicide researchers. A significant portion of parricides are one-on-one, meaning that one offender (usually a teenage male) kills the victim (father/mother) during the course of an argument, robbery, or other largely unknown (that is, unknown to the police at the time of filing of the report) events (Shon & Targonski). Hence, although the psychoanalytic dimensions of the motive themselves are still complex, the exclusive character and range of victims preclude other dynamics that may operate in the crime: certain assumptions about the nature of homicides are taken for granted.

In this paper I look at homicide cases that do not have a clear and distinct one-on-one victim/offender relationship: mass murder. Using the Columbine High School incident as a case example, I argue for the need to make distinctions within homicide events; and once victims, both intended and actualized, are examined psychoanalytically, the simplistic assumptions of one-on-one homicides become evident. Looking at cases of mass murder, victimology (and other situational characteristics of the crime), informed by Lacanian psychoanalytic theory, may reveal several dynamics concurrently operating within one homicide event. Before a researcher can uncover any of the dynamics at work, she first runs into a practical problem: what type of homicide is it? Just as the identities of the participants of one-on-one homicides are murky, the classification of certain mass murders is problematic. The Columbine event is just such a case. But before we make any speculations, we have to establish the apparent facts of the case. Since I do not have access to police or coroner's records and was not on the scene to interview witnesses, my data is limited to what I was able to discern from initial news coverage of the incident and from interviews with witnesses, victims, survivors, friends, and acquaintances of the offenders.

Runaways, the Deadlock of Youth Care Services

Iris De Groote

Iris De Groote

Iris De Groote   Assistant professor in the Department of Psychoanalysis and Clinical Consulting, and is a member of the Research Unit Psychoanalytical and Psychodynamic Studies at the University of Ghent (Belgium). She is a practicing psychoanalyst and a founding member of a supervision group for starting therapists. She has done research by government order on runaways and the disappearance of minors. Her interests focus on Youth Care Services and more recently on outcome studies.

Introduction

In 1995 the National Center for Health Statistics published a report about health-risk behaviors among American youth. This report shows that about one in six teenagers had run away at least once in the course of a year, and boys were more likely than girls to have done so (17.5% versus 14.1%). The study states that there are about half a million runaways in the United States of America. Other estimates are as high as two million. There are many confounding factors when accurately counting these youth. About thirty-five percent of the runaways have already run away before, even several times. Furthermore, they are then unlikely to reside in adult shelters, where such data are collected. Federally funded shelters are estimated to serve only one in twelve runaway youth. To make a complete count, one would be required to account for those living independently in streets, parks, train or bus stations, subways, abandoned buildings (“squats”), and stranger's homes (Farrow 720). It goes without saying that living at such at-risk locations makes them more easily victims of sexual, physical, and emotional abuse. In the United States assaults, illness, or suicide will take the lives of 5,000 runaway youth each year (National Runaway Switchboard).

The Council of Europe estimates that in the United Kingdom approximately 40,000 minors run away every year. In Germany the number of runaways is even higher. The best “guestimate” indicates there are 7,000 street children in the Netherlands, 4,000 in Belgium, 10,000 in France, 500 to 1,000 in Ireland, and 6,000 to 7,000 in Turkey. The majority of runaways are between 13 and 17 years old (65.8%), particularly above the age of 15 (Council of Europe). Once these youth are on the streets, there are few legitimate means of survival. Although some try various kinds of delinquent activity such as selling drugs, stealing, and panhandling, one of the most common ways of obtaining funds is through “survival sex.” Street youth often exchange sexual activity for food, shelter, drugs, or protection from someone who is older and more streetwise. Many youth have little or no knowledge of prostitution when they first reach the street, but after talking with involved peers who seem to be making easy money, it becomes less frightening. Especially in the largest urban areas, the number of street youth involved in prostitution is high.

Popular Culture, Psychoanalysis, and Pedagogy: An Exploration of Citizenship

Doug Zook

Doug Zook

Doug Zook   Assistant Professor of Education at the University of Regina, Regina, Saskatchewan, Canada, where he teaches courses on social studies education and curriculum. He is currently exploring how the intersections of critical citizenship education and popular culture can be interpreted through a psychoanalytic framework.

At this present time both the nation I am from, Canada, and the nation I am currently living in, the United States, are holding national elections. While the forms of democratic practice are different—one is parliamentary and the other congressional/republican—the goal of having citizens become involved in decision making through their elected representatives is shared. It is an exciting time for social studies teachers in both nations; it provides flesh to the bones of printed textbooks, bringing to life the concepts of democratic principles we so often extol. But during these times and other less adrenalin-inspired ones, how can social studies teachers engage their students with important considerations of citizenship? What kinds of possibilities might exist? Are there some pedagogical practices that can be articulated?

The context from which this paper is drawn is from doctoral research that has attempted to address the question: How can films be used to explore the idea of responsible-active citizenship within a critically informed psychoanalytic practice? This research has consisted of examining literature in the areas of social studies, citizenship, postmodernism/poststructuralism, psychoanalysis, and film theory. The individuals who agreed to take part in the study—high school students (n=66), their teachers (n=2), and post-secondary students (n=6)—provided a welcomed opportunity for a novice researcher to pursue his inquiries. Together we engaged for a short time in a process to explore the possibilities for engaging in dialogue, using filmic texts as a base, which might lead to possibilities for active citizenship.1 This research was intended to expand knowledge and practice for the social studies classroom.2 In this intention I have been deeply taught. I have wrestled with ideas for a pedagogy that has resulted in more questions than answers. Martusewicz (102) explores how to love the questions, even the disconcerting ones, and comments that “we learn that while we want to know, our knowing is limited by the tools that we have at our disposal, the relation between our ability to name and to perceive, for example.” The experience of this naming and perceiving has become a lived experience, though limited by my own (inabilities and (mis)perceptions as they traverse my subjectivity as a teacher-researcher.

Concerning the Status and the Function of Theory in the Formation of the Psychoanalyst

Frédéric Declercq

Frédéric Declercq

Frédéric Declercq   Assistant Professor of Clinical Psychology and psychoanalysis at the State University of Ghent (Belgium) and a practicing psychoanalyst. He has published a book and several articles on Lacan's category of the Real with respect to the discussion of trauma and the final phase of the analytical treatment.

Desire to Know and Horror to Know

One of Lacan's major theses with regard to knowledge states that the desire to know can be a transvestite of the horror to know. According to Lacan, the search for and the accumulation of knowledge can be nothing but an attempt to run from truths the subject does not want to know. Indeed, it is an attested clinical fact that the truth can be kept hidden—that is can be kept unconscious—through a body of theoretical knowledge (Ecrits 358). This mechanism works in the two directions: by means of knowledge, one can run from one's own truth as well as from the truth of somebody else.

Concerning the first case, Lacan demonstrated that a number of theories come down to recycled unanalysed unconscious material, meaning that unconscious psychical contents have been recycled into theoretical knowledge. To quote Lacan:

I could do an analysis of Abraham for you simply on the basis of his theory of part-objects…. Abraham, we might say, wanted to be a complete mother. Then I might also amuse myself by punctuating the fringes of Ferenczi's theory with a famous song by Georgius ‘I am son-father.’ Nunberg, too, has his own intentions, and in his truly remarkable article on love and transference, he shows himself to be in the position of arbiter between the powers of life and death, in which one cannot fail to see an aspiration to the Divine position. (Four 158-159)

According to Lacan, knowledge might very well be the symptom of one's ignorance. As a matter of fact, Lacan points out the mechanism of symptom formation in the heart of the elaboration of a theory. This means that he recognises the mechanisms of repression and the return of the repressed in the constitution of the theory as such. More particularly: a psychic content is repressed and it reappears in an unrecognisable form. In this case, the return of the repressed has taken the form of a theory.

The same mechanism can be traced easily within an analysis too, and especially within a so-called didactic analysis. I think it is safe to say that every psychoanalyst has had the experience of an analysand starting to elaborate a theory or applying concepts to himself, whether they be psychoanalytic, philosophical, or other ones. During such a process, the analyst will have noticed the very particular moment when the analysand starts doing this: these reactions take place when some repressed content is being approached too closely. It is at that precise point, when the associations come too close to a point of truth, that the patient starts applying theory to himself and tries to analyse himself as if he were someone else. Theory as a return of the repressed also explains the well known phenomenon that students in psychoanalysis will really understand their own paper a couple of years later, while doing or after having done an analysis.

Christopher Breu

Christopher Breu

Christopher Breu   Assistant Professor of English at Illinois State University, where he teaches courses on twentieth-century American literature, popular culture, and critical and cultural theory. He has published on subjects as diverse as Maryse Conde's Moi, Tituba, Sorcière … Noire de Salem, and contemporary techno and indie rock. He is currently completing work on a book manuscript entitled “Hard-Boiled Masculinities: Fantasizing Gender in American Literature and Popular Culture, 1920-1945.”

Did Somebody Say Totalitarianism? Five Interventions In The (Mis) Use of a Notion is the latest theoretical Molotov cocktail lobbed by Slavoj Žižek in the guerilla war against neo-liberal hegemony and what he views as the forms of postmodern theoretical and cultural cynicism that underwrite it. Žižek has emerged in the last ten years as one of the Euro-American academy's most prominent theorists, leading the charge against what was the hegemony of poststructuralism and de-construction in the late 80s and early 90s and spearheading a return to what he describes as the “twin materialisms” of psychoanalysis and Marxism.

In some ways, Žižek, as a disciple of Lacan, seems like a strange theorist to be leading this charge. Until recently, the conventional wisdom has been that the Lacanian revolution in psychoanalytic theory was essentially a linguistic one, in which Lacan reworked the insights of both Freud and Saussure to produce an account of the subject's emergence in and formation by language. This account of subjectivity seemed fully congruent with the basic tenets of post-structuralism, and many cultural theorists took it as such, deploying a Lacanian account of subjectivity along with a Foucauldian or Derridian account of social power in order to provide a fully working model of the intersection of subjectivity and the social.

In key works such as The Sublime Object of Ideology and Tarrying With the Negative, Žižek challenged this conventional wisdom, arguing that, as Louis Althusser recognized in the 1970s, Lacanian psychoanalysis has more in common with the forms of Marxist critique rejected by most post-structuralists than it does with poststructuralism itself. The reason that this was not evident to most Anglo-American readers of Lacan is that, with the exception of Seminars XI (The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis) and XX (On Feminine Sexuality), only the early, predominantly structuralist, seminars and writings of Lacan have been translated into English. The later Lacan, Žižek argues, was less concerned with the linguistic structuration of the domain of cultural meaning which Lacan terms the Symbolic and more concerned with the unsymbolizable knot of contradiction that organizes the social field as such, which he terms the Real. Žižek describes the Lacanian Real in a somewhat contradictory fashion as both a void and a domain of uncoded materiality, but it is the latter form of the Real on which his argument hinges. Forms of materiality that are uncoded in the symbolic, such as the “raw flesh of blood and muscle” that lies behind the mask of our socially coded face, come to occupy the space of the Real and represent the locus of social contradiction; Žižek offers a memorable description of this process in a reading of John Woo's Face Off that serves as a critique of Levinas' and Derrida's reading of the ethics of the face (Totalitarianism 182). It is this Lacanian turn to “materiality” that Žižek argues is congruent with Marxist conceptions of materiality and which, along with the latter, can be used to challenge what he sees as the neo-idealism of much of post-structuralist theory.

Cynthia Burack

Cynthia Burack

Cynthia Burack   Associate Professor in the Department of Women's Studies at The Ohio State University. She is the author of The Problem of the Passions: Feminism, Psychoanalysis, and Social Theory (New York University Press) and articles in feminist theory and political psychology.

In the 1980s, the social debate over child sexual abuse and its effects, particularly for women, escalated in the form of a debate over what came to be called “recovered memory.” Many adults came to understand themselves as survivors of childhood sexual abuse, and although they did not have continuous memories of early abuse, they relied upon recovered memory to reconstruct past events. For those elders who now stand accused of sexual crimes against children, faith in recovered memory is misplaced; for them, a biased therapeutic establishment encourages the fabrication of “false memory.” In Pillar of Salt, Janice Haaken, a professor of psychology and clinical psychologist in private practice, intervenes in this highly charged debate. Refusing to take sides, she examines the debate itself, including its psychological, cultural, and historical dimensions. The results of her study are unlikely to comfort those who have taken up opposing positions, but they do throw considerable light on the issues for those who remain on the sidelines.

Haaken begins by examining women's vexed relationships to memory and remembering, framing the analysis around the biblical story of Lot's wife. The nameless woman, turned by God into a pillar of salt for looking back on the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, is punished more mercilessly than the husband who attempts to barter their daughters to appease a sexual mob. What is so threatening, Haaken asks, about women “looking back”—acting as the purveyors of memory, especially memories of patriarchal abuses? In responding to that question, Haaken addresses both feminist attempts to reify women's recovered narratives of abuse as unimpeachable truth and false memory critics' attempts to impeach women's narratives of intrusion, harm, loss, and voicelessness. Her exploration takes her into topics that are the stuff of scholarship as well as headlines: hysteria, posttraumatic stress disorder, multiple personality disorder, spiritualism, and charges of satanic ritual abuse.

I

The relationship between psychoanalysis and medicine is not a simple one. Historically, the origins of psychoanalysis refer to a failure of knowledge; in his quest for truth, Freud worked through this shortcoming to discover the Unconscious at the same time that he established its method of exploration. Fragments of the former knowledge—i.e., Medicine—were dragged over to the new discipline, modifying their meaning substantially (e.g., the terms symptom, trauma, and many others, do not mean the same in each of the two discourses).

The Writing Cure poses interesting and ambitious questions while at the same time presenting a view of the field of composition that both challenges and defends some of the major assumptions currently published and taught by professionals

in the field. Perhaps the most ambitious, and most appealing for those inclined toward a psychoanalytic approach to writing instruction, is Bracher's grappling with the social constructionist hegemony in composition instruction and theory. Bracher does not use the term “hegemony,” but he spends the first section of the book building up a strong argument against the powerful claim to exclusive theoretical and political correctness in the composition classroom that social constructionism has had in the past few years. At the same time, he explains and defends a Lacanian psychoanalytic approach to teaching writing while, if not exactly defending expressionist teachers, at least commending the expressionist approach for coming closer to the therapeutic and meliorative aims of psychoanalytic pedagogy than social constructionists could possibly achieve.

Why Use Psychoanalytic Approaches to Writing?

Bracher's argument proceeds thus: He notes first that writing and psychoanalysis belong together because “a psychoanalytic perspective can offer unique and valuable insights into (a) central but often hidden forces operating in the writing process, (b) the sources of writing problems, and (c) the dynamics of writing instruction” (1). He then explains away possible objections that teachers are not analysts and should not be doing what they are not trained to do. His response to this objection is that they already are working in the realm of psychoanalysis, whether they use expressivist techniques or social constructionist approaches. He confronts the desirability of social constructionism in the teaching of writing by arguing that social constructionist classrooms can investigate areas such as date rape or even more sensitive social issues that can be quite upsetting, yet teachers in these classrooms usually have no understanding of the psychological impact of these topics on writers. He moves on to issues of power and dismisses this problem by noting that power is more diffuse in a caring, concerned classroom than in a classroom that features critical and confrontational pedagogy.

Racial Castration: Managing Masculinity in Asian America is a thought-provoking and innovative collection of literary interpretations, motivated by Eng's timely and necessary imperative to connect the foundations of racism with the foundations of sexual difference and its ideological demands of heterosexuality. The analytical device Eng uses to assemble these connections is psychoanalysis. His task is difficult but urgent, given that psychoanalysis' historical assumption that sexual difference is the fundamental human experience of difference limits its relevance to racial subject formation.

Eng's introduction, “Racial Castration,” foregrounds the need to support yet deviate from psychoanalytic tenets in theorizing Asian American masculinity:

I am interested in the ways in which [psychoanalysis] might be creatively deployed to leverage a more thorough understanding of the psychic burdens and material costs imposed on the Asian American male subject who aspires to assimilate into mainstream society. What is psychically required of the Asian American male subject who desires to be part of the dominant mainstream society? How is the Asian American male subject encouraged or coerced to see himself in a social order governed by race and racism? How does he unconsciously or unwittingly contribute to the perpetuation of his already contested existence? (23)

Eng responds to these questions with readings of several Asian American fictional pieces, films, and scholarly debates. He treats these cultural objects as testimonials to the already present linkages between politics, history, and individuality. Such a focused approach allows him to present the significance of a raced psychoanalysis in vivid and concrete situations. As such, the richest and most thought-provoking displays of Eng's creative intervention are to be found in these localized interpretations.

The first chapter, “I've Been (Re) Working on the Railroad: Photography and National History in China Men and Donald Duk,” examines Maxine Hong Kingston's China Men and Frank Chin's small book, Donald Duk.

David Mann MD

David Mann

David Mann   Practices psychiatry and psychoanalysis in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is a former Fulbright Scholar in cybernetics and theoretical biology, a member of the Board of Directors of the Massachusetts Institute for Psychoanalysis, and teaches at Harvard Medical School. He has authored numerous articles on philosophical and clinical aspects of psychiatry and psychoanalysis, and a book on the metastructure of psychodynamics, A Simple Theory of the Self (Norton, 1994).

Neurosis and Addiction

Psychoanalysis arose from the need for a nineteenth-century medical approach to neurosis, that baffling state of the self-identified patient whose medical-seeming symptoms revealed no apparent organic cause, often appeared somehow unwittingly self-induced, impressed many observers as less painful than meaningful, and seemed to mean, in particular, something about sex—earning such conditions since ancient times the cognomen “hysteria.”

What has become of neurosis? In our day it has all but vanished from popular as well as professional discourse. Psychic suffering has taken on a new mantle of medical meaning, now more frankly psychological in its presentation but still cloaked in the medical “in-valid-ation” that serves in some measure to protect its sufferers from appearing either to have brought it upon themselves, or to mean anything by it. Instead of neurosis we now have Disorders. In place of hysteria, neurasthenia, and obsessional neurosis we now encounter Depressive Disorder, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, Attention-Deficit Disorder, etc., all very scientifically categorized to five significant figures and supported by scientific data popularly taken to prove that the sufferer's brain is doing it all to him—as many Disorders, an alien or merely cynical observer might say, as there are ways to lose the capacity to tolerate one's passions, to lose or even abdicate agency over them, or to make sense of them, as the now-unfashionable psychoanalytic psychiatry once tried to do. Today, instead of exploring symptoms to find their meaning, we classify them. Instead of explaining them, we try to undo them with drugs. If thine eye offend thee, pluck it out! When we do explain symptoms—and by “we” I mean primarily contemporary psychiatrists and those who share their general perspective on these matters—we follow the psychoanalyst's lead by imputing those symptoms to unconscious processes; but we go further than the analysts and locate the processes deep in the dynamic unconscious, beneath the psychological altogether, in the tissue and chemistry of the brain, a giant step further into dualism. “It's not me, It's my chemical imbalance,” becomes the erstwhile neurotic's complaint. And his defense attorney's. And that of the prosecutor who holds the psychiatrist liable for the murder the patient committed because his drugs were given wrongly. And wins. When we mistake the correlates for the causes of experience and behavior, we place the subject beyond responsibility for his own experiences and deeds, the unwitting plaything of his brain. Character is no longer fate. Anatomy is destiny once again. The now-benighted notion of unconscious motivation reduces, in the conception of modern psychiatry, to a kind of neo-phrenology of cerebral determinism.

Introduction

Many contemporary psychoanalytic authors discuss the scientific status of their discipline. The general tenor of these discussions is that psychoanalysts should concentrate on the scientific foundations of psychoanalysis. This work is necessary in order to assure the position of psychoanalysis within its classical domain of application (clinical work) and within an academic context. In both domains psychoanalysis is often criticized on not being scientific. A remarkable trend in these discussions is the tendency to reduce science to statistically based research. Another remarkable trend is that especially non-Anglo-Saxon European psychoanalysts criticize this tendency (cf. Dreher, Perron, Green in: Sandler et al.). According to them the field of science is broader than statistically based research. Several theories in the philosophy of science support this point of view (Dreher). Specific alternative research strategies within the domain of psychoanalysis nevertheless are to be developed.

In this paper I reflect on one alternative approach: qualitative interview research. First of all, I consider qualitative research, and secondly I relate it to psychoanalysis in general and especially to Lacanian psychoanalysis. As you will see, on the one hand I agree with the idea that psychoanalysis should question and study its scientific status by means of research. On the other hand, I think that the kind of research we engage in should be in accordance with a broader theory of the relation between science and psychoanalysis.

I think the considerations I propose can help us in developing a research methodology that fits psychoanalysis in its application to psychological, social, cultural studies.

Qualitative Research …

Outside of the evolutions within psychoanalysis, methodologists have developed a number of research strategies for the social and the human sciences known as qualitative research. Within this field, different methodological and theoretical approaches co-exist.

Relationality and Prejudice

A half century ago, in the preface to his classic book The Nature of Prejudice, Gordon Allport alluded to the relational quality of human nature. He stated, “Human nature seems, on the whole, to prefer the sight of kindness and friendliness to the sight of cruelty” (xiii). At that time, the relational perspective was only beginning to be formulated, yet his comment can be integrated into a movement which has a principle suggesting that human behavior is motivated to establish and maintain relationships with others. If this premise is acceptable, than it is possible to speculate that behavior that is contrary to a relational orientation may be pathological. Prejudicial behavior has this pathological quality, the impact of which is at both the interpersonal and macrosocial levels. Given that object relations theory comments about the relational development of persons, as well as the psychopathology of poor relational abilities, it stands to reason that object relations theory may inform our effort to understand and perhaps address the development and maintenance of prejudice.

Throughout the twentieth century a variety of psychodynamic explanations were offered to explain prejudice. Duckitt found that following World War II efforts were directed at understanding the unconscious motivations of prejudice. These involved defense mechanisms as the universal processes that can explain the pervasive nature of prejudice. The psychodynamic perspective of this period suggested that defense mechanisms, such as displacement and projection, permitted unconscious internal conflicts to be expressed as prejudice toward outgroups. Research findings were not decisive, and efforts shifted from emphasizing process to structure in an effort to explain prejudice as an outcome of a personality structure. The authoritarian personality emerged as the prototype of this kind of person (Adorno, Frenkel-Brunswick, Levinson, and Sanford). Duckitt suggested that the lack of empirical support and poor ability of the theory of the authoritarian personality to explain widespread prejudice in whole societies prompted another shift in emphasis toward a sociological understanding.

Janice Haaken

Janice Haaken

Janice Haaken   Professor of psychology at Portland State University and a clinical psychologist in private practice. She has written extensively on psychoanalysis and feminism, gender and trauma, and the psychology of social movements. Haaken is author of Pillar of Salt: Gender, Memory and the Perils of looking Back and is currently writing a book on women, aggression, and psychoanalytic social theory.

There are different kinds of feminists, drawn to the movement for a range of personal reasons. For some, it is the maternal side of female social bonds, the warm conviviality of women's gatherings. For me it was solidarity with other women who, as girls, got into trouble for talking back. In my family, the punishment for talking back was having your mouth washed out with soap. It was not for many years that I recognized the exquisite logic operating here, how the punishment perfectly conformed to the crime. With spanking, the ritual centered on a humiliating and controlled exercise of pure submission. I remember very few spankings. With the soap punishment, aggression on both sides—on that of the victim as well as that of the torturer—was permitted. It is quite difficult to force a slippery object into the mouth of a resistant child, so this ritual could easily fall apart midway through the procedure. More importantly, resistance was expected. The victim could scream and writhe when that half-gelatinous bar of Ivory was forcefully crammed inside her mouth, glazing her teeth. She could spit to rid herself of the horrible bitterness, without this act of defiant indignation being viewed as an invitation for more punishment.

In looking back, I can see how this punishment operated within the social symbolic order of bourgeois womanhood—with maternal aggression expressed within a framework of maintaining domestic hygiene. But I also came to view it in terms of what classical psychoanalysts call “oral rage.” Just as Victorians created highly sexualized subjects through their obsessive preoccupation with control over the body, as Foucault so famously argues, mothers like mine may have created girls with dirty mouths.

These were also moments of enacting the perverse strains in mother/daughter relationships. The thrusting of an unwelcome object into a body orifice was part of a larger world of intimate invasions, a sense of perpetual vulnerability to being penetrated by an Other, either literally or metaphorically. But my mother—generally not intrusive—focused on the mouth as the site of both resistance and desire. For she was, herself, terrified of speaking in front of strangers, much less talking back.

Introduction

What follows is a transcript of the plenary panel on Psychoanalytic and Psycho-Social Studies in the United Kingdom held at the eighth annual APCS conference at Rutgers last November. I think it felt quite strange for us to be invited over in some sense because we spent several hours talking about ourselves, our institutions, our projects, and sometimes our anecdotal experiences of teaching psychoanalysis in higher education, rather than delivering academic papers. In other words, we were not quite sure what we were going to do and say. What transpired, we feel, was a very constructive dialogue between ourselves and colleagues in APCS and from around the world. Some very important issues were raised about the relationship between practitioners and academics, between the vocational and the purely theoretical. It was also noted that there were quite distinctive differences between projects and departments in Britain and those in North America—not least, the long tradition in the United Kingdom of cultural Marxism, social administration, and social history which forms a backdrop to the teaching of psychoanalysis in many sociology departments. I think that probably the most important aspect or theme that emerged from the evening was to see difference and differences between institutions as a positive thing which we can learn from, and help each other develop programs and links. This panel, for example, is entirely Kleinian in its psychoanalytic persuasion, but there was a noticeable lack of disagreement between psychoanalytic schools of thought and more of an emphasis on the interpenetration of psychoanalysis and the social and political. This, for me, has been one of the major themes (and attractions) of JPCS over the last few years, and in some sense this gelled on that evening at Rutgers last year.

This paper is set out in the discursive style of the panel presentation. I start by giving an overview of the institutions and people involved in the panel. Karl Figlio then goes on to talk about developments in teaching psychoanalysis at the University of Essex, where he is Director of the Centre. Karl, who has many years experience of teaching psychoanalytic studies, outlines the relationship between academics, practitioners, and institutions in the United Kingdom. Heather Price then goes on to talk about her experiences of teaching psychoanalytic and psycho-social studies at the University of East London and Tavistock Clinic. Heather's observations are set out in a separate paper which proceeds this text. The final speaker, John Bird gives an outline of the development of a new venture at the University of the West of England, a Centre for Psycho-Social Studies which has grown out of the successful activities of a small group of researchers and academics interested in the intersection between the social, the political, and the psyche. The paper concludes by highlighting some of the questions and themes that were raised in the post-plenary discussion.
