Introduction

In the post-war period, psychoanalytic theory has seen a significant paradigm shift from the drive-based individual of traditional Freudian theory to an emphasis on the importance of relationships for understanding individual agency (Aron; Benjamin, 1 Bonds; Ogden). A core proposition of this relational psychoanalysis can be summed up in the phrase unconscious intersubjectivity, by which is meant the unconscious dynamics that work between people to constitute their experiences of self, others, and their capacity to act in the world. In this paper we use the case study of one heterosexual couple, Juliet and Billy, in order to explore and develop the potential of this principle of unconscious intersubjectivity in research into relationships. Specifically, we argue that it helps us to unravel certain paradoxes which emerge in the accounts produced from two interviews with each person.

The interviews were gathered during a study of gender differences in the fear of crime on one high-crime and one low-crime public housing estate in the north of England.1 One thing that became clear in our research was that the general term “fear of crime” was misleading: people fear particular crimes, and in the case of Juliet and Billy, we focus on burglary and on their shared fear of Juliet being the victim of a sexual crime.

Following from our relational psychoanalytic starting point, we reasoned that, in the case of heterosexual couples, their different relations to fear of crime might have to do with the complex intersubjective dynamics of living in a highly gender-differentiated world. Specifically, we expected that the discourses and patriarchal relations contributing to fear of crime offer up different positions to men and women: broadly speaking, fear for women and the capacity to protect for men. However, discursive explanations of this type have been criticized for not acknowledging the role of an active subject. In our framework, we ask what motivates the take-up of these gendered positions and how relational dynamics affect such investments. In heterosexual couples, we are likely to be looking at investments in gendered identities—masculinity and femininity—and how these are secured relationally.

To Discover

In the first chapter of his book The Conquest of America, Tzvetan Todorov offers a brief account of the discovery and suppression of difference at the beginning of the modern era. His subject is Columbus, an explorer of the unknown who finds only what he already knew.

Todorov begins with the motive that drives Columbus to undertake his hazardous travels to the New World. In the matter of motives, of course, the pursuit of gold looms large, and much evidence can be marshaled to support the claim that desire for riches sets Columbus in motion. Yet, in the end, Todorov rejects this motive, or at least insists that it remains subordinate to another, which is the “universal victory of Christianity” (10). Columbus and others of his time believed that opening a western route to the orient would make it possible for Christians to “recover the Holy Land and send the Turks reeling back to central Asia” (Morrison 16). The triumph of Christianity would, of course, require a substantial amount of wealth. As a goal, it is consistent, therefore, with the pursuit of riches, though it makes that pursuit a means rather than an end in itself.

Though gold and God play a large part in motivating the voyage of discovery, Todorov also discerns another motive, one closer to the spirit of the modern age, as pursuit of the glory of God expresses the spirit of an older time. This other motive treats discovery not as a means but as an end in itself (13). Discovery as an end in itself differs essentially from discovery as a route to establish the hegemony of God in the universe. While the former remains open to possibilities as yet unknown, the latter does not, since to imagine we might discover what is not known is to challenge the word of God, and the order set in place by Him. Columbus finds himself caught between the two possibilities, which is to say between the traditional and the modern worlds.

The whole idea of discovery depends on the unknown, without which there is nothing to discover. The idea of the unknown is also the essential premise of modernity. Yet Columbus, the most famous of discoverers, cannot accept this idea. As Todorov points out: “He knows in advance what he will find; the concrete experience is there to reveal a truth already possessed, not to be interrogated according to pre-established rules in order to seek the truth” (17). To seek the truth means to accept that we do not know it, which Columbus cannot do. Thus, since Columbus must find the civilizations of the Orient, he makes his crew swear an oath that they will find civilized inhabitants in the New World, and fines those who dare give voice to any doubts on the matter, as if expressing doubt could in itself undermine the discovery of the truths already known (Todorov 22). For Columbus, doubt is the enemy of truth, an attitude that contrasts sharply with one that would make doubt the starting point for discovering truth.

If there is indeed some truth to Freud's Copernican revolution, then ethics and morality are in serious jeopardy. According to the basic Freudian conception of human nature, all facets of subjectivity are ultimately derivatives of or reactions to the conflict between “the two principles of mental functioning,” namely, the pleasure principle and the reality principle. Human nature contains no innate ethico-moral sentiments, no intrinsic conceptions of goodness, justice, respect, or virtue. The infantile organism enters the world as nothing more than a bundle of drives, an aggregate of mechanistic sexual and aggressive tendencies. The sole rules governing this id-creature are the dynamics of the primary processes and the libidinal law of pleasure. Gradually, the constraints imposed upon this being by the reality principle (defined as all the various hindrances, both natural and cultural, to the pursuit of pleasure) hammer into shape a socialized subject that appears to operate in accordance with the norms and values of his/her social milieu. The journey from infantile organism to socialized subject is, in Freudian parlance, nothing other than the trajectory running from id to superego.

In “Kant avec Sade,” Lacan, appearing to echo Freud's suspicions about the origins and motives of ethico-moral intentionality, raises the issue of the status of the “voice of conscience,” the internal enunciator of the moral law. In his system of pure practical reason, Immanuel Kant takes for granted the reliability of this inner monologue subtending ethical decisions. The voice of conscience is assumed to be the trustworthy direct delegate of the moral law, unproblematically guaranteeing the ethical worth of the subject's acts. Lacan accuses Kant of having neglected to explore the phenomenality of the voice itself, treating the voice of conscience as if it were purely formal/noumenal.

Psychoanalytic Culture gives an impressively comprehensive survey of figures who have used psychoanalytic concepts to explore contemporary cultural phenomena. Part One discusses some of Freud's writings on culture, Group Psychology and Totem and Taboo, and his theory of drive, primarily as Freud set it out in “Instincts and Their Vicissitudes,” and how these writings got taken up by a tradition of object relations psychoanalysis, including such analysts as Bion, Wolfenstein, Winnicott, and Klein. Part Two discusses the Frankfurt School's reliance on Freud's writings on culture to develop Marxist critiques of ideology. This section focuses on figures from the Frankfurt School including Adorno, Horkheimer, Benjamin, Marcuse, Fromm, Reich, and Habermas. This part ends with a chapter that proposes the French postmodernist Baudrillard to be “part of this tradition as exemplar and symptom of its decay and excess” who “both celebrates and sabotages the attempt by the Frankfurt School to go beyond action to praxis” (109, emphasis Parker's). Part Three focuses on Lacanian psychoanalysis, its relations to linguistics, and how Lacan's concepts develop in the work of figures such as Althusser, Kristeva, Laplanche, and Žižek.

Susan Gutwill MS LCSW CTT and Nancy Hollander

Nancy Hollander

Nancy Hollander  

Politically informed psychoanalytic theory has much to contribute to a discussion of how people internalize the social structures and media messages of their culture. While most current psychoanalytic theories emphasize the impact of actual relationships on the intrapsychic life of individuals and on the intersubjective space they inhabit, few examine the direct impact of the cultural surround on each of us. However, just as Donald Winnicott suggested that there is no infant without the mother, we contend that there is no mother-child dyad, no family triad, without its larger cultural surround—that is, what is sometimes referred to as the culture mother, culture parent, culture home or the second family. The elements of culture to which we apply psychoanalytic theory in this paper are (1) the impact of symbolic media violence and actual violence on the conscious and unconscious minds of children and (2) the efficacy of programs developed to ameliorate their harmful effects.

Violence in the Mass Media

By the time a middle-class child in the U.S. graduates from high school, having spent approximately 13,000 hours in school, she or he will have watched 18,000 hours of television (an average of four hours a day) and 22,000 hours if the child has grown up in poverty. When the average child reaches the age of six, she will have spent more time watching TV than she will spend in talking to her father in a lifetime. American television is the most violent in the world. The typical American child witnesses 12,000 violent acts on television every year, and will see 8,000 simulated murders before s/he finishes elementary school. Saturday morning cartoons are even more violent than most adult shows, averaging over twenty violent acts per hour (Majority Staff, Senate Committee on the Judiciary; Karla Kalin).

Young people represent the major consumers of films and video games, as well. Today's typical cinematic fare offers ubiquitous images of the stabbing, shooting, abuse and torture of innocent men, women, and children. Film-goers are increasingly saturated by horrific “entertainment” with a host of antiheroes who are sick, unkillable, psychopathic, and evil. While traditional horror stories and films facilitated the working through of unconscious fears symbolized by mythic but unreal monsters who were exorcised, in today's horror films terror is personified by characters who resemble our neighbors and co-workers, who are not killed but rather return over and over again to menace us. Increasingly, movie heroes implement vigilante justice, acting on their own outside the framework of the law. Their individualistic retaliatory violent behavior is justified by the depiction, in gruesome detail, of villains' cruel assaults on innocent victims. This perverse entertainment is consumed by adolescents along with the powerful rewards of group companionship, physiological stimulation of candy and soft drinks, and the intimate physical contact of a boyfriend or girlfriend. Thus, this contemporary film experience conditions teenagers to associate extreme violence with the narcissistic pleasures of food, social bonding, and sexuality (Grossman).

One form of psychoanalytic social criticism locates an object central to political and social issues

156

and then describes how that object becomes a repository of various fantasy projections that govern or dictate fantasmatic rather than just or realistic relations with that object. For instance, Elisabeth Young-Bruehl's The Anatomy of Prejudices describes how anti-semitism, racism, homophobia, and sexism are the expression of classes of fantasies generated by cultural and personal history. In her analysis, particular groupings of people are assigned a role in the fantasy script of a dominant culture. In another analysis, Lewis D. Wurgraft's The Imperial Imagination describes how British-ruled India, as an object, served a fantasy space for the acting out of primitive magical thought and narcissistic fantasy. Quoting Geza Roheim that “our first responses to the frustration of reality is magic” (55), Wurgraft documents how British citizens repeatedly found India a place of romance, magic, and enchantment. Karl Figlio's book follows a similar analysis, but its object of focus offers a more complex and elusive object for analysis: nature, the natural world, the inanimate ground of scientific study.

Figlio situates his work neatly in relation to some noteworthy philosophical and historical issues. What allowed the shift in the Western world to a modern worldview that grasps nature as an inanimate object, whereas before nature had always been animate, alive, filled with gods and spirits and supernatural forces? Figlio points out that Freud usefully described our view of reality changing as the result of three great blows to our narcissism. The first was our recognition through Copernicus that we were not at the center of the universe. The second was Darwin's suggestion that we were not fundamentally different from animals. The third was Freud's argument that we were not masters of our conscious minds. To these three wounds, Figlio wants to add a fourth: “There is a fourth blow to narcissism which Freud explored but did not list with these three upheavals: nature is not a mother, and the natural world is indifferent to mankind” (61).

Diane Simmons

Diane Simmons

Diane Simmons   Books on Jamaica Kincaid and Maxine Hong Kingston were published in 1994 and 1999, respectively. She is currently at work on a book-length study of the psychological roots of British imperialism as seen though literature. She is an assistant professor of English at the Borough of Manhattan Community College, City University of New York.

In recent years there has been a great deal of work that invites us to explore the psychology fueling European imperialism and the racist attitudes that accompanied it. In the years after World War II, post-colonial writers have portrayed European imperialists as psychically empty and lost, clinging desperately to the pedestals of grandiosity they had built for themselves. As early as 1963, Albert Memmi, in Colonized and Colonizer, painted the European ruler in North Africa as a person at home nowhere, deeply conflicted in the role of colonial master, knowing within himself that the superiority he claimed was a sham (58). Ngugi wa Thiong'o has portrayed the English in Kenya as similarly displaced, alienated from home and god, sustained only by their ability to dominate others (76). More recently West Indian writer Jamaica Kincaid has described the imperialist as one who may have “fashioned for himself a body of steel,” but whose hard shell conceals an interior that is dead and decaying (76).

Also fairly recently, students of imperialist literature have found evidence that it was not only a desire for material gain which drove Europeans to dominate other peoples both literally and imaginatively. This literature, which reveals the psychological landscapes of those wielding or imagining imperial power, often, as Sara Suleri writes in The Rhetoric of English India, “reorganizes the materiality of colonialism into a narrative of perpetual longing and perpetual loss” (10). Elleke Boehmer, in Colonial and Post-colonial Literature: Migrant Metaphors, shows that even as the European imperialist rejects the native, “he also requires the native's presence in order to experience to the full his own being” (63). And Patrick Brantlinger, in Rule of Darkness: British Literature and Imperialism, has explored the way in which deeds of empire, as portrayed in nineteenth-century adventure literature, provides a world of opportunity for “white heroes, usually free from the complexities of relations with white women” (11). The imperial relationship, as it emerges from these texts, is often described as narcissistic, and repeatedly the imperialist is shown using his subject in an attempt to realize himself. By subjugating the native, Abdul R. Jan Mohamed writes, the European is able to “compel the Other's recognition of him and, in the process, allow his own identity to become deeply dependent on his position as a master. This enforced recognition from the Other in fact amounts to the European's narcissistic self-recognition” (85). These studies suggest, as Homi Bhabha has written, that the politics of race “will not be entirely contained within the humanist myth of man or economic necessity or historical progress, for its psychic affects question such forms of determinism. Social sovereignty and human subjectivity are only realizable in the order of otherness” (61).

When I was asked to speak at a meeting about violence, I expressed quite a bit of initial hesitation. In part it was because I automatically assumed that I had to speak about how one ought to work with violent patients. “Who am I,” I asked myself, “even to speak about working with violent patients, let alone to suggest a model treatment approach?” After all, like most full-time private-practice psychoanalysts, my contact with physically violent patients has been rather limited compared, for example, with that of a staff therapist at Rikers Island or at the lock-up ward at Bellevue. But I didn't say no right away and I soon found myself thinking about the differences between aggression and violence in clinical work. I was thinking about how they could both be pretty scary. The primitive rage of a frustrated narcissist or the depth of aggression in certain borderline patients can often be very difficult to tolerate, but the way it is frightening for the therapist differs considerably from the kind of anxiety we feel in the presence of an actively violent patient. What got me thinking about this was remembering a consultation I once had with a man who, quite convincingly, told me that he murdered a girlfriend—a murder that he was never held to account for—while in the midst of an acute paranoid psychosis. From the story he told, I believed him. Whether or not this was a sign of gullibility on my part is certainly open to question, but the fact of the matter was that I did believe him. The reason he scheduled a consultation with me was that he feared he was decompensating and about to once again become actively psychotic. As best I could tell he was correctly assessing his situation, and the last thing in the world I wanted, at a time like that, was to become an important transference figure in his turbulent emotional life! So I told him about all the reasons why I was not the best choice of therapists for him, and got him out of the office as soon as I could. He really scared me, and I felt a great relief when he agreed that a psychiatrist who knew how to do psychotherapy, but who also could prescribe medication for him, might be able to be more helpful to him. My point thus far is not that this was an incorrect recommendation, but that I made it out of fear rather than out of conviction. And what is even more important about this is that I think it indicated a kind of counter-transference that is different from the typical counter-transferences I am more used to being plagued by when I an working with characterologically disordered people who, despite the primitivity of their aggression, do not seem likely to be actively, physically violent.

I would like to say a few words about my conscious motivation to write this paper. I came to the United States from China to study psychotherapy two years ago. I had become interested in the psychoanalytic perspective on human behavior in my late teens, when I was in college for medical science. I took some classes related to the theory and techniques of psychoanalytic therapy. After a brief review of ego psychology, we discussed mainly contemporary object-relations theory, self psychology, and the recent relational movement in the field. In these theories, the Freudian concept of the superego is infrequently discussed or even neglected. It seems to me that this contemporary psychoanalytic emphasis—or lack of it—fits the American culture, which fosters and values individualism. The individualized self and its relationships comprise the main units of analysis. Even in the relational and intersubjective movements, individualistic assumptions dominate current psychoanalytic discourse. It is assumed, for example, that whenever a person makes a decision, the initial motivation is the satisfaction of personal needs and desires, especially instant needs. Possible outcomes of efforts to realize one's individual aims, especially outcomes that affect others, might not be considered carefully until the need-satisfying action has occurred.

Chinese people, in contrast, value collectivism and tend to think constantly about possible outcomes, especially those that would affect others. Before even conceptualizing, much less pursuing, individual satisfactions that would have a direct or indirect impact on others, they would think collectively. Their strong superego would prevent a lot of impulsive acting out and would also inhibit some decisions that might lead to individual benefits. It seems to me that Freud's structural theory can be usefully applied to Chinese behavior, perhaps at least partly because social constraints in China are not entirely different from the very structured, post-Victorian Vienna of Freud's times. Although China is undergoing dramatic changes, especially in its big cities, most of its regions are still traditional in both lifestyle and attitude. It seems to me that the ways in which behavior is regulated in America and in China are different. I have found it personally useful to try to understand these differences in terms of alternative superego structures.

Generally, psychoactive medicines are thought to possess the virtue of facilitating, preparing, or even opening the field where analytic working through, or something like it, might develop. It is also argued of “mental illness” that it should be considered a solid, objective, and objectifiable entity (e. g., through objective measurement techniques such as multicentric questionnaires). Therefore, apart from and beyond objectified suffering (or its side of jouissance), the illness is supposed to exist as a foreign body, and the pharmacological object is ready to attack it. Likewise, beyond the signifier (a phobic fantasm, an obsessive ritual, the “pain of being”) lie the neurotransmitters, this new metamorphosis of the old hypothesis of an organic disorder. If the brain must then be considered thought's material support, if the “verifiable facts” command, must then thought itself admit that the power of the neurotransmitters precedes and makes words possible? A psychoanalyst working as a Liaison-Consultant at a Public Hospital stands between different worlds, an incessant confrontation between Psychoanalysis and Medicine, between the field where subjectivity may briefly appear as a glimpse and Science, which necessarily excludes the individual. Psychiatry, as a by-product of Medicine that cannot preclude subjectivity otherwise than by trickster tricks (psychoactive medicine being one of the most conspicuous of these), is a controversial affair which shall be questioned here from a psychoanalytic outlook, taking several observations as a starting point.

A Liaison-Consultation is demanded in an inpatient department; the patient has a former diagnosis of bipolar disorder. The interview takes place in her room, where she lies in her bed, her sister at her side. Between them stands the small night table, on top of which is a display of the medicines she takes. These are in adequate correspondence with her diagnosis: torrents of lithium, streams of carbamazepine, waves of chlonazepam.

Large organizations of the twenty-first century will continue to rely on time-tested forms of organizational structure perfected during the twentieth century. The most numerous of these organization forms is the hierarchical organizational structure, where layer upon layer of positions are depicted in the familiar chart of organization (see Figure 1). These organizational tables array positions downward from a single position containing the most organizational power and authority to those with the least. The single position at the top of these charts, the chief executive officer position (CEO), is understood to contain within it the ultimate responsibility for the organization's performance and with this responsibility ultimate decision-making power and final authority. It is also understood that as one descends the hierarchy the amount of decision-making power and authority diminishes to the point where, near the bottom, employees may very well have no formal decision-making power or authority relative to even the smallest task that they perform.

Hierarchical organizations are, however, much more than a multi-layered organization form that arrays positions by their importance, power, and authority on a vertical axis. A second equally important attribute is that they are divided up on a horizontal axis, as any inspection of a traditional organization chart reveals (see Figure 1). Large organizations contain many areas of specialization, such as finance, accounting, marketing, legal and information services, research and development, production, and human resources, to list but some of the most common divisions arrayed on this horizontal axis. Additionally, within some of these divisions there may occur further horizontal subdivisions based on specialization and breaking the workforce down into more manageable subsets based on the size of the work units. A paper mill, for example, may have many teams of individuals doing the exact same work but on different machines.

Let us now attempt to wash our brains clean of all we have heard about Antigone and look in detail at what goes on there.

—Lacan, Ethics 250

The tragic is the expression of the absolute position.

—Hegel, in Hippolyte 341

Lacan with Hegel, or the Ethics of Tragedy

Because tragedy, and more specifically Sophoclean tragedy, is the genre privileged above all others by both speculative philosophy and psychoanalytic theory, it should come as no surprise that the tragic ethos permeates the dialectical structures of both discourses, particularly in their ethical modes. Famously, Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit bases its analysis of the dialectic of ethical substance in the Ancient world on the Antigone of Sophocles.1 Less famously outside French analytic circles, Jacques Lacan's seminar on the ethics of psychoanalysis (1959-1960) culminates in a difficult but spellbinding reading of that exemplary tragedy. As Suzanne Gearhart has argued, speculative philosophy and Freudian psychoanalysis “are modeled after and elaborated to an important extent in terms of a particular view of tragedy” (1). One of Lacan's main intentions, however, in revisiting Sophocles was to draw a line of demarcation between his own interpretation and Hegel's. The object of this essay will be to perform a close reading of Lacan's interpretation of Antigone in the view of distinguishing it from its Hegelian predecessor, elucidating the stakes involved in the Lacanian articulation of psychoanalytic ethics, and exploring the concept of tragedy through which Lacan's argument takes shape. Though Lacan's reading of Antigone forms the coda of his attempt to outline a psychoanalytic ethics, this element of the seminar has yet to find the sustained discussion it deserves.2 What follows will begin to spell out the nature of the politically radical challenge Lacanian ethics mounts against the identitarian, conformist, and market-driven ethic of liberal tolerance and multiculturalism—what Lacan calls in the seminar the “service of goods” (303)—that predominates in today's North American academy.

This is why I have tried to think of God in terms of desire, a desire that cannot be fulfilled or satisfied…. In this sense, our desire for God is without end or term: it is interminable and infinite because God reveals himself as absence rather than presence.

—Emmanuel Levinas, Ethics of the Infinity.

I would like to know whom or what he [Moses] faced on Sinai and on Horeb. But after all, since he couldn't bear the brilliance of the face of him who said “I am what I am,” we will simply say at this point that the burning bush was Moses's Thing [das Ding], and leave it there.

—Jacques Lacan, The Ethics of Psychoanalysis.

I remember a friend saying to me several years ago, “What prevents the face of the other in Levinas from being das Ding?” I didn't know quite what he meant at the time, but the question was clearly meant critically. I would like to answer the question directly now by saying that nothing prevents the face of the other being das Ding…

—Simon Critchley, Ethics, Politics, Subjectivity.

In a paper originally presented at the first “God and Postmodernism” Conference at Villanova University, Richard Kearney thematized the “Desire of God” in a way that paved the grounds to re-pose the same question by taking it a step further: if nothing prevents the other from turning into the monstrous site of the Thing, then what prevents God, as the absolute other, from being das Ding. How can we distinguish the Levinasian God from the Lacanian Thing? What can assure us that, within the ethical relationship with the Other, we will not find ourselves “vis-à-vis” not with a face but with the voracious emptiness of the Thing? And how can we know that our desire is a desire toward God (à Dieu) and not the metonymic desire that takes its leave (adieu) away from him?

References to Lacan in Kearney's paper were explicitly made only once (Desire of God 116). Lacan's ghost, however, haunts the text. Lacanian trademark terms such as the concept of desire as lack (112, 116), the lost object (116), manque-à-être (117, 120), and the nom-du-père (120) are to be found in a number of places and always in contradistinction to Levinas. Why did Kearney choose Lacan to pair with Levinas in his analysis of divine desire? Lacan's and Levinas' world-views seem incompatible, if not antithetical, to each other; their understandings of subjectivity, alterity, and language look like two parallel lines that run together but never meet. And yet, it seems that there is something in these two proper names, and the systems that they represent, that challenges Kearney to attempt this curious conjecture, Levinas and Lacan, if only in order to intensify their differences. Their possible encounter was situated by Kearney on the threshold between “two different ways of desiring God” (112)-that is, the onto-theological and the eschatological desire. In what is to follow I will try to untangle the problematics developed between these two kinds of desire as they are exposed in the “Desire of God” and in the “Ethics of the Infinity,” a dialogue that took place between Kearney and Levinas in 1981.

Introduction

Before the child knows sexual difference as the anatomical difference between the sexes, the child knows or recognizes the lack in the mother's desire for something that the father is perceived as having. The anatomical discovery of the difference between the sexes (“show me yours and I will show you mine”) will be placed within this symbolic context. Thus, more than a penis and before it is a penis, the phallus is a signifier of a lack within the mother's desire. Within Lacanian theory, the symbolic and imaginary significance of the phallus have ascendancy over its anatomical function.

If it is true, as Lacan says, that it is the subject's relationship to the phallus that determines sexual position, then it is also true that within Lacanian theory, the significance of the presence and absence of the phallus is a multilayered dialectic across the three registers of experience. The phallus is the signifier of the desire of the Other, of what the mother desires from the father. For Lacan the phallic function is equivalent to the function of castration defined as a symbolic lack of an imaginary object. Thus, the imaginary phallus is the contextual object that in the Oedipal crucible is construed as what the father has which the mother wants. The imaginary phallus, as such, does not exist because the symbolic phallus is a missing phallus and castration as a symbolic act bears not on the penis as a real organ, but on the imaginary phallus. For Lacan, symbolic castration refers more to a fact of the structure rather than to a biological fact or to an imaginary or traumatic threat. From a Lacanian perspective, the old psychoanalytic interpretation of castration as representing the biological or constitutional inferiority of women appears as a dated fiction or imaginary construction. The concept of castration is not the bad thing that in the West we have come to associate with a rejection of femininity. The concept of castration as a biological form of inferiority mimics the view of femininity as the second or weak sex that prevails within what Lacan called the master's discourse. Lacan was able to avoid the imaginary interpretation of the complex by theorizing the three registers and giving Freud's concept its specific weight and symbolic significance.

The International Association of Relational Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy (IARPP) is a professional/intellectual community of individuals, clinicians and non clinicians who identify with and/or are interested in the sea change that has pervaded the worlds of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy in recent years. Its goal is to create a space for an open, democratic community of creative and rigorous thinkers and practitioners. Its ethos is a love of learning, not the consolidation of any particular discipline or any professional interest group. Its vision is to evolve as a collective think tank, adding energy to existing organizations rather than competing with them, and drawing on the perspectives of those in related, non-clinical fields of interest. The Association will make it possible for individuals in different contexts and locales to share common interests, experiences, and resources. It will sponsor real-time and cyber gatherings.

The first of these gatherings, and the launching of the IARPP, was initiated by the Stephen A. Mitchell Center for Relational Psychoanalysis. A major conference, entitled “Relational Analysts at Work: Sense and Sensibility, A Conference in Memory of Stephen A. Mitchell,” was held January 18-20, 2002 in New York City. Its aim was to provide a forum within which a relational approach to clinical work could be articulated and discussed. Drawing an audience of over 1000, the conference was regarded as a landmark event, the launching of an intellectual space which for many has become the psychoanalytic home they have been seeking for a long time.

One of the pillars of relational psychoanalysis as viewed by the IARPP is a commitment to building a community of thinkers that is not defined by privilege or discriminatory practices. The IARPP intends to address any underrepre-sentation directly and to invite those who feel underrepresented to join in thinking about the issues involved. The IARPP provides a forum for dialogue and debate about any and all contemporary issues in psychoanalysis, from all segments of the psychoanalytic community without regard to age, citizenship status, color, disability, marital or parental status, national origin, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

Like Emmanuel Levinas, D. W. Winnicott is a great critic of totalization, the reduction of the other to the same, the bringing of everything that is new and different under my categories. For both (though only Levinas makes it a philosophical problem), totalization is the legacy of Western rationalism, that knows only via the subsumption of the particular by the universal.

I recently published an article in which I compared Levinas and Winnicott on the concept of violence. For both, violence is totalization, the subsumption (for Winnicott it is an assumption) that the other is just like me. Certainly the violence that Levinas writes about sounds like the violence of the intrusive mother, the mother who is out of tune with the child. Is it too strong to call this violence? Not for Levinas, and not for a host of postmoderns, for whom even writing is a violent act, fixing a shimmering subjectivity forever. Levinas puts it this way on the first page of Totality and Infinity:

Violence does not consist so much in injuring and annihilating persons as in interrupting their continuity, making them play roles in which they no longer recognize themselves, making them betray not only commitments but their own substance, making them carry out actions that will destroy every possibility for action. (21)

No concept was more important to Winnicott than the interrupted continuity to which Levinas refers. Winnicott was preoccupied with gaps and spaces: the gaps and spaces in the experience of the self that arise from a lack of attunement by mother and others, as though one's self had disappeared along with mother, a gap in going-on-being.

The burden of my article was that the transitional relationships about which Winnicott writes, relationships marked by the reluctance to ask who's who and what's what, were not likely to foster totalization. Levinas was assuming that human psychology operated according to strict cleavages: if other was not absolutely other, then it must be the same as me.

She specializes in contemporary political theory, focusing on feminist thought, critical theory, postmodernism, and psychoanalysis. Her book Voluptuous Yearnings: A Feminist Theory of the Obscene offers a reading of obscenity that combines these critical venues. She is currently working on a study of how Theodor Adorno's writings prove useful to feminist scholarship.

American culture currently exhibits an ever deepening interest in the “cunning, baffling” nature of addiction, and has begun to speak about this malady in something other than shaming, moralistic terms. Americans are now more aware of how the addict's often subtle pathology enacts the logic of Derrida's pharmakon, the charming, perfidious substance that both heals and infects, both sedates and attacks, both entraps and induces a wonderful catharsis (Derrida). This dastardly, ambivalent nature of the pharmakon, the “poisoned present” whose magic is lethal, only adds to its mystique, and addiction's pharmacotic structure ensures that its ravaging impact goes hand in hand with an array of euphoric, empowering pleasures. Indeed, the many outgrowths of Alcoholics Anonymous witnessed in such twelve-step programs as Al-Anon, Narc-Anon, Smokers Anonymous, and Overeaters Anonymous have changed the tenor of our discussion surrounding the profound malaise made manifest in addiction.

In keeping with the cunning logic of this malady, those relationships that deteriorate into a tragic dependency often begin much like a love affair, bringing with them a magnificent sense of personal exaltation, a feeling of freedom and ease that helps assuage a battery of underlying insecurities. Many recovering addicts recount that the initial stages of a tawdry dependency often feel like falling in love, for they involve a newfound attachment that brings with it a joyful, brimming sensation, a euphoric release from life's harsher realities. In his biography of Bill Wilson, a cofounder of Alcoholics Anonymous, for instance, Robert Thompson describes the rapturous sense that Wilson first had when he discovered the pleasures of inebriation: alcohol had more than befriended him, it had become a lover who met his emotional and physical needs on the deepest level. It had become an intimate companion whom he could count on to make him feel good.

It was a miracle. There was no other word. A miracle that was affecting him mentally, physically, and, as he would soon learn, spiritually too…. [A] t his back, he could hear the whine of the saxophone, little waves of voices rising, falling, but now they in no way ran against the overwhelming joy he was feeling. His world was all around him, young and fresh and loving, and as he made his way down the drive he moved easily, gracefully, as though—he knew exactly how he felt—all his life he had been living in chains. Now he was free. (Qtd. in Kurtz 14)

Fairbairn's Theory of Object Relations

Thomas Oberlechner

Thomas Oberlechner

Thomas Oberlechner   Clinical psychologist and mentor of the psychology program at Webster University in Vienna. He holds degrees from University of Vienna (MA, JD, PhD) and Harvard University (EdM), where he studied object relations theory with George W. Goethals. He is a training psychotherapist for the Association for Rogerian Psychotherapy in Vienna and is currently a Visiting Scholar at the Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University.

Ronald Fairbairn's writings show that he has very carefully assimilated Freud's classical theory. However, struck by the significance of object relationships in the treatment of schizoid patients, he departs from classical psychoanalytic theory in a number of critical respects. Fairbairn expresses his highly original and intellectually vigorous ideas on human personality in a series of papers from 1940 onward (Sutherland, “Obituary” and “British”). His theory forms the foundation for some of the most significant advancements in contemporary psychoanalysis. The core of Fairbairn's theory is the notion that psychic structure, the self, is based directly on the vicissitudes of object relatedness (Rubens).

The present overview of Fairbairn's theory of object relations focuses on four theoretical cornerstones upon which his psychoanalytical thinking rests. These foundations include (1) Fairbairn's description of the schizoid personality as found in Schizoid Factors in the Personality, (2) the psychoanalytic development from classical libido theory to object relations theory, (3) Fairbairn's theory of the development of human object relationships, both described in A Revised Psychopathology of the Psychoses and Psychoneuroses, and (4) Fairbairn's revision of the mental apparatus which conceptualizes the basic endopsychic structure as a multiplicity of egos. Fairbairn's views regarding the mental structure are most clearly stated in Endopsychic Structure Considered in Terms of Object-Relationships.

The Schizoid Personality

The study of schizoid patients led Fairbairn to the conclusion that their etiology lies in the mother's failure to give the infant an adequate experience of “being loved for himself.” Thus Fairbairn sees the basis of healthy development not in the satisfaction of instincts, but in the passing on to the infant that it is a person and that it is loved as such. When deprived of this experience, the child becomes too frightened to make object relations. The child fears that its love will be rejected, and builds up a compensatory world of inner objects and relationships. The unitary ego of the infant, which is present from the beginning, becomes massively split (Guntrip).
